approach_variants.name: Stuart Lake Trail, the first switchback and Mountaineer Creek
approach_variants.notes: A short technical route with a rough approach in front of it. From the Stuart Lake Trailhead at the end of Forest Road 7601 off Icicle Creek Road, take trail 1599 to the fork at about 4,500 ft and keep right for Stuart Lake. Carry on through the beaver meadows and leave the trail at the first switchback, where it quits the flats and starts climbing to the lake; how far past the fork that is depends on who you ask, anywhere from half a mile to a mile and a half, so navigate by the swamp and the switchback rather than by the odometer. Cross the Stuart Lake outlet on logs and work south up the Mountaineer Creek drainage with the creek on your left. The path has not been maintained in a very long time: blowdown, re-routes, slide alder, boulder fields and cairns that lead somewhere else. Follow the drainage up to a flat area around 5,800 ft in the basin between Sherpa and Argonaut, which is where nearly everyone camps. The climb above is snow or ice to about 50 degrees, taken with pickets and the odd screw on a running belay, then a scramble to the summit. Most parties reverse the couloir, which is slow and slushy work in the afternoon; the alternative is to drop the far side of the ridge and come back around the rock ribs to the low pass between Sherpa and Argonaut. Carry two tools, a small rack to three inches, and expect the descent to take longer than the climb.
hazards: Rockfall funnelled down a scoured chute in the middle of the couloir, worse as the face warms
Snow and ice conditions that vary enormously year to year and even day to day
Runout snow averaging 45 degrees with steeper steps, where a slip is not stoppable
A thin mixed section low in the couloir when it is lean
Unmaintained approach with heavy blowdown, slide alder and boulder fields
Creek crossings on logs, considerably worse during runoff
Exposed chimneys and a slabby summit traverse above the couloir, often in mountaineering boots
approach_variants.baseFinding: The decisive mistake on this route is made low down, at a fork in Mountaineer Creek, and by the time you can see a couloir you have already made it. Work up the drainage and take the SOUTH, climber's-left branch into the basin between Sherpa and Argonaut, camping on the flat around 5,800 ft. The other branch leads north-west to a basin near 5,400 ft under the Sherpa and Ice Cliff glaciers, which is Mount Stuart's north face, and the big obvious couloir up there tops out at a col at about 8,600 ft on Stuart's east ridge — a fine climb, on the wrong mountain. At least one party has gone up the wrong branch and had to cross a buttress to correct it, and accounts differ on whether there are two branches or three, so count carefully and ignore the cairns, which lead toward Stuart. From the correct basin the northeast face carries several gullies and no verbal description separates them cleanly. What identifies this one is the approach to it and what it opens onto. The couloir is entered after about 1,000 ft of scree, rock and gravel up an obvious avalanche path, it runs roughly 1,000 ft at an average of 45 degrees, and it usually has a scoured channel cut down its middle that rockfall follows, which is both the confirmation and the thing to stay out of. It tops out in a NOTCH on Sherpa's east ridge at about 8,000 ft, and from that notch the balanced rock is in plain view along the ridge. That is the check: notch with the balanced rock in sight, not a col with Mount Stuart rising beyond it. Above the notch expect a class four chimney with old rappel slings in it, a harder chimney with a move or two of mid-fifth, a tunnel to pass through, then a traverse on the north side of the crest to the top rather than one short 5.0 pitch. The true summit is the west block; the free-standing pillar across the notch beside it is about two feet lower and much harder, needing a shoulder stand and an old bolt, so you do not have to climb it.

itinerary.cal: The NNE gully and upper basin often hold snow into early-mid summer; an ice axe (and sometimes crampons) can be useful before roughly July, and the Icicle Creek Road to the Stuart Lake TH is open year-round.

days.note: This is done as one long day from the Stuart Lake trailhead, not a backpack — parties hike the maintained trail, peel off onto a rough climbers' path into the Sherpa-Argonaut basin, climb a class 3-4 gully to the ridge, traverse to the block, do the short 5.7 shoulder-stand/friction move and rappel off the fixed anchor, then reverse the whole approach. Total round trip is roughly 14 miles with about 5,000 ft of gain and loss (trailhead ~3,600 ft to the 8,605 ft high point).

schedule.label: Leave Stuart Lake trailhead
schedule.detail: Most parties start pre-dawn by headlamp given the length of the day.

schedule.label: Leave the maintained trail
schedule.detail: Branch onto the unmaintained climbers' path toward Sherpa-Argonaut basin; expect brush and downed timber.

schedule.label: Enter Sherpa-Argonaut basin (~7,000 ft)
schedule.detail: Begin the broad NNE-trending gully toward the ridge crest east of the balanced rock.

schedule.label: Gain the ridge, traverse to the block
schedule.detail: Class 3-4 travel over blocks and sandy benches west along the ridge to the base of the balanced rock.

schedule.label: Climb and rappel the block
schedule.detail: Shoulder-stand/friction pitch (5.7) to the top, then rappel from the fixed anchor back to the ledge.

schedule.label: Reverse the route to the car
schedule.detail: Down the ridge, gully, and basin, back onto the Stuart Lake Trail to the trailhead, typically finishing in daylight or early evening for parties that keep moving.

days.objective: Tag the Sherpa Balanced Rock summit block via the NNE gully and ridge traverse

itinerary.totalNote: A long single day: about 14 miles round trip with ~5,000 ft of gain and loss, including a short 5.7 shoulder-stand pitch and rappel; fit parties that don't linger finish car-to-car in roughly 10-13 hours.

access.fees: Northwest Forest Pass required to park at the Esmeralda/Longs Pass Trailhead (Ingalls Way TH) — $5 single-day or $30 annual.
access.notes: 2026 lottery application window Feb 15–Mar 1 (results after Mar 17, accept/pay by Mar 31). ~25% of overnight slots also released as a walk-up daily lottery the day before entry. Season requiring the overnight permit: May 15–Oct 31. A single-day ascent with no camp inside the boundary never needs the lottery.
access.rules: Standard Alpine Lakes Wilderness regulations apply: Leave No Trace, wilderness group-size limits, and (in the core Enchantments zones) campfire restrictions — verify current forest orders.
access.permit: Falls within the Enchantment Permit Area's Stuart Zone. Day trips only need a free self-issue wilderness day-use permit at the trailhead. Overnight camping in the basin between May 15 and Oct 31 requires a paid overnight permit ($5/person/day, groups up to 8) obtained via the Recreation.gov Enchantment Permit lottery or walk-up availability; outside that quota window no overnight permit is required.
access.closures: No route-specific closures found for North Fork Teanaway Road/FR 9737 to the Esmeralda Trailhead; this route does not use the Icicle Creek Road corridor. Check current Okanogan-Wenatchee NF (Cle Elum Ranger District) alerts before driving in.

before.fa: Fred Dunham, Ray Lilleby, James Wick — August 13, 1961
before.approach: Start at the Longs Pass Trailhead (Esmeralda TH) at the end of Teanaway River Road (USFS Rd 9737) out of the North Fork Teanaway. Take Longs Pass Trail #1229 climbing steadily through open pine forest and sagebrush switchbacks for about 2.5 miles and 1,950 ft of gain (roughly 1.5-2 hours) to Longs Pass at approximately 6,200-6,400 ft, which opens up the first views of Mount Stuart, Ingalls Peak, and the Stuart Range crest. From the pass, drop off the north side on a steep, loose, eroded boot path (sometimes called the 'tapeworm') losing about 1,400-1,600 ft over roughly a mile to Ingalls Creek at about 4,800 ft; this descent tread is dirt/scree and can be slick and hard on the knees. Ford Ingalls Creek (a rock-hop in low water, but a genuine wet crossing during early-season snowmelt) and pick up the Ingalls Creek Trail, following it west/upstream about half a mile to the Beverly-Turnpike Trail junction at roughly 4,700 ft - the last dependable water source before the alpine basin above. From the junction, a climbers' boot path (referenced in trip reports as 'Variation #1' toward Mount Stuart) switchbacks up through forest and talus; around 6,000 ft it narrows into a gully system. Traverse east several hundred feet to a divide separating two gullies, then drop into the eastern gully, which leads more directly toward Sherpa Peak. Class 2 slopes above the gully lead to 'Table Rock,' a large flat boulder at about 7,400 ft in the boulder-choked Sherpa-Argonaut basin, a common high bivy for parties splitting the approach over two days. From Table Rock, a short Class 3 scramble gains a notch just west of Sherpa's summit on the Stuart Range divide, putting climbers on the ridge crest east of the balanced rock; follow the crest west over blocks and sandy, exposed benches (Class 3-4) to reach the base of the balanced rock formation itself, where the Standard Route begins with a shoulder-stand or rope-lasso move to gain the east-side pedestal, then bolt-protected friction climbing (5.7) to the summit block. Car-to-base is roughly 6-7 miles one-way with close to 4,500 ft of cumulative elevation change; expect loose rock and real route-finding through the gully/basin section, and carry all the water you'll need above the Beverly-Turnpike junction since the upper basin is dry.
before.rappels: 4 single-rope rappels down the ascent route
